title: WHO WAS HUR? THE FORGOTTEN MAN WHO HELD UP MOSES’ HANDS WHEN ISRAEL’S FUTURE HUNG IN THE BALANCE
paragraphs: WHO WAS HUR? THE FORGOTTEN MAN WHO HELD UP MOSES’ HANDS WHEN ISRAEL’S FUTURE HUNG IN THE BALANCE

He never parted the Red Sea. He never received the Ten Commandments. He never stood before Pharaoh. But on a battlefield where exhausted hands began to fall, this almost-forgotten man helped hold the line—and revealed a truth every weary Christian desperately needs to hear.
What if one of the most important things God ever calls you to do is something the world will never applaud?
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
It is the exhaustion of being the one everyone depends on.
The mother who keeps praying for a child who seems determined to destroy his own future.
The father who smiles at the dinner table while silently wondering how he will pay the bills.
The pastor who preaches about hope on Sunday and fights discouragement on Monday.
The believer who encourages everyone else but secretly wonders why nobody notices that their own hands are trembling.
You still believe in God.
You still love Jesus.
You still want to be faithful.
But somewhere between the prayers that seem unanswered, the responsibilities that never stop, and the battles nobody knows you are fighting, something inside you has begun to whisper:
“Lord, I don't know how much longer I can keep my hands raised.”
And that is where a man named Hur enters the story.
Not with a sword.
Not with a thunderous prophecy.
Not with a spectacular miracle.
He enters the story with something much quieter.
He notices that a man of God is getting tired. And instead of criticizing his weakness, he helps carry the weight.
His name appears in a few verses of Scripture, but the lesson of his faithfulness reaches far beyond that ancient battlefield.
And perhaps the most astonishing part of his story is not what Hur accomplished.
It is what might have happened if he had decided that helping someone else was beneath him.
Because sometimes, while everyone is watching the battle, God is working through the people holding up the hands of those who can no longer stand alone.
Israel had only recently experienced one of the greatest deliverances in biblical history.
God had brought His people out of Egypt.
The sea had opened before them.
Their enemies had been overwhelmed.
They had witnessed the power of the Lord in ways that generations would remember.
Yet deliverance from Egypt did not mean they would never face another battle.
That is a truth many believers discover painfully.
You can be genuinely saved and still encounter suffering.
You can walk in obedience and still face opposition.
You can experience God's faithfulness yesterday and still need His sustaining grace today.
In Exodus 17, the Israelites were at Rephidim.
They had already struggled with thirst and questioned whether the Lord was among them.
Then another crisis arrived.
The Amalekites came and fought against Israel.
This was not a comfortable moment for a nation learning to live in freedom.
These were people who had spent generations under oppression. They were now confronted by an enemy in the wilderness.
Moses instructed Joshua to choose men and go out to fight.
Then Moses made a remarkable declaration:
“Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand.” — Exodus 17:9, KJV
Joshua would fight below.
Moses would stand above.
And two other men would accompany him.
Aaron.
And Hur.
Most Christians recognize Aaron.
He was Moses' brother, a central figure in Israel's deliverance and the man who would become Israel's first high priest.
But Hur?
Who was he?
Where did he come from?
Why was he standing beside Moses at such a decisive moment?
And why does Scripture tell us so little about someone who played such an important supporting role?
The honest answer is that the Bible does not provide a complete biography of Hur.

Exodus 17 identifies him as one of the two men who accompanied Moses onto the hill. Exodus 24:14 later shows Aaron and Hur entrusted with responsibility among the elders while Moses went up the mountain.
That is significant.
Hur was not merely a random spectator who happened to be nearby.
He was someone Moses trusted enough to bring into a critical moment and later name alongside Aaron in a position of responsibility.
But Scripture does not tell us exactly how Hur came to hold that position.
Some Jewish traditions identify him as Miriam's husband, which would make him Moses' brother-in-law. However, this relationship is not explicitly established in the biblical text.

Exodus 31:2 names a Hur in the ancestry of Bezalel, the gifted craftsman appointed for the work of the tabernacle, and 1 Chronicles 2:19–20 records a Hur in that same family line. These passages are commonly connected with the Hur of Exodus 17, but Scripture does not explicitly state that the men are identical.
We should be careful here.
Faithfulness to God's Word means refusing to turn an interesting tradition into a biblical certainty.
We do not need to invent Hur's background to appreciate his obedience.
What Scripture actually tells us is already powerful enough.
Because on that hill, Hur did something that many people overlook until they find themselves desperately needing someone to do the same for them.
Listen carefully to what happened.
“And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.” — Exodus 17:11, KJV
Imagine the scene.
Below the hill, swords clash.
Men struggle for their lives.
Dust rises from the battlefield.
Joshua and the Israelites fight against an enemy determined to overcome them.
Above the battlefield stands Moses, holding the staff associated with God's mighty acts of deliverance.
As his hand remains raised, Israel gains the advantage.
But when his hand falls, Amalek begins to prevail.
Then Scripture records a small sentence with enormous emotional weight.
“But Moses' hands were heavy.” — Exodus 17:12, KJV
Read that again.
Moses' hands were heavy.
The man who had confronted Pharaoh.
The man who had stretched out his hand over the sea.
The man through whom God had performed extraordinary signs.
The man entrusted with leading an entire nation.
That man grew tired.
There is something deeply comforting about the Bible's refusal to hide the limitations of its human servants.
Moses was chosen.
Moses was called.
Moses was used mightily by God.
And Moses still had physical limits.
His calling did not make his muscles inexhaustible.
His leadership did not make his body invincible.
His experience of miracles did not remove his need for help.
Perhaps someone reading this needs to understand that distinction.
Being weary does not automatically mean you are being unfaithful.
Sometimes you are tired because you have been carrying real responsibilities for a long time.
Sometimes the answer is not another accusation against yourself.
Sometimes you need rest.
Sometimes you need wise counsel.
Sometimes you need a brother or sister in Christ who will sit beside you and help you endure.
Moses' hands were heavy.
But thank God, Moses was not alone.
Exodus 17:12 continues:

“And they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.”
What a picture.
They brought a stone.
They gave Moses somewhere to sit.
Then Aaron stood on one side.
Hur stood on the other.
And together, they supported his hands.
Notice what they did not do.
They did not shame Moses for becoming exhausted.
They did not tell him that a stronger leader would never need assistance.
They did not abandon him when his strength began to fail.
They did not compete to see who could receive the most recognition.
They responded to the need directly in front of them.
And the battle continued.
There is a beautiful detail in the original Hebrew that deserves our attention.
The Hebrew expression translated “his hands were steady” is:
וַיְהִי יָדָיו אֱמוּנָה
Vayhi yadav emunah.
The final word, אֱמוּנָה (emunah), carries the sense of firmness, steadiness, reliability, or faithfulness.
In this particular verse, it describes the steadiness of Moses' hands.
It would be inaccurate to claim that the Hebrew literally says Aaron and Hur transferred their faith into Moses or that the word necessarily means spiritual faith in this context.
But the picture is still extraordinary.
Hands that had become heavy were made steady through the practical support of others.
And there is something profoundly moving about that.
The text does not say Moses suddenly received superhuman strength.
It says Aaron and Hur held him up.
God's purposes were being accomplished in a scene where human weakness was met with faithful assistance.
And sometimes that is exactly how the Lord cares for His people.
Not always by removing every burden instantly.
Sometimes by providing people who help us carry it.
Perhaps you have been asking God to make you stronger, while overlooking the faithful people He has placed beside you.
Or perhaps you are the one God is calling to become that kind of support for somebody else.
The friend who notices when another believer has become unusually quiet.
The husband who sees that his wife is overwhelmed and chooses to serve instead of complain.
The wife who stands faithfully beside her husband through a difficult season without pretending his struggles are insignificant.
The church member who prays for a discouraged pastor instead of joining every conversation that tears him down.
The believer who checks on the person who always says, “I'm fine,” because something in their eyes suggests otherwise.
You may never stand on a platform.
You may never preach to thousands.
You may never receive public recognition for the sacrifices you make.
But do not confuse visibility with faithfulness.
Heaven's standard of greatness is not the same as the world's appetite for applause.
And now we come to something even more important.
We must not read Exodus 17 as though Moses' raised hands were a magical technique that forced God to give Israel victory.
The biblical account does not explicitly say Moses was praying throughout the entire battle, although his posture has often been understood as an expression of dependence upon God.
The staff in his hand was not an object possessing independent supernatural power.
The power belonged to the Lord.
That becomes unmistakably clear when the battle ends.
Exodus 17:13 tells us that Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
Joshua fought.
Moses stood.
Aaron and Hur supported him.
But the story does not conclude with a monument to Joshua's military skill or a celebration of Hur's personal greatness.
Instead, Moses built an altar.
And he gave it a name.
יְהוָה נִסִּי
YHWH Nissi.
“The LORD is my banner.” — Exodus 17:15
There is the heart of the story.
Not Moses is my banner.
Not Joshua is my banner.
Not Aaron is my banner.
Not Hur is my banner.
The LORD is my banner.
Israel's victory was ultimately attributed to God.
Every human participant had a role, but none of them deserved the glory that belonged to the Lord.
And this is where the story begins to confront us.
Because there is a temptation hidden inside Christian service.
We may begin by wanting God to be glorified.
Then slowly, almost without noticing, we begin to crave recognition for our part in His work.
We want someone to notice the hours.
The sacrifices.
The money given.
The prayers whispered.
The ministry responsibilities carried.
The things we gave up so someone else could move forward.
And when nobody notices, resentment begins to grow.
Why does everyone thank the person on the platform?
Why does nobody remember the person who helped them get there?
Why does somebody else receive the credit for work I helped make possible?
Hur's story confronts that hunger for applause.
The biblical narrative gives us no recorded speech from Hur on the hill.
No dramatic declaration.
No personal testimony explaining his emotions.
No account of him demanding acknowledgment afterward.
We cannot claim to know everything he thought or felt.
But we can see what he did.
He stayed.
He supported.
He helped Moses endure until sunset.
And the Lord's name was lifted high.
What if that is enough?
What if some of the most beautiful acts of Christian faithfulness are the ones performed without an audience?
Jesus spoke directly to the danger of doing righteous things merely to be seen by people.
In Matthew 6, He warned against practicing acts of righteousness for human applause.
He taught His disciples that the Father sees what is done in secret.
That truth changes everything.
Because the unseen life is not unseen to God.
The quiet prayer is not wasted.
The hidden sacrifice is not forgotten.
The act of mercy that receives no public recognition is still known to the Father.
But this passage also contains a warning for anyone who has been trying to become everyone's Hur.
You are not the Savior.
You cannot carry every person's burdens indefinitely.
You cannot solve every crisis.
You cannot heal every wound.
You cannot make another person's decisions for them.
And you cannot take the place of Jesus Christ in somebody's life.
Even Hur's help had a particular purpose, in a particular moment, within the work God was accomplishing.
Biblical service is not a command to destroy yourself through endless responsibility.
Galatians 6:2 calls believers to bear one another's burdens.
Yet Galatians 6:5 also speaks of each person bearing their own load.
Christian love involves both compassionate support and responsible stewardship.
Sometimes helping means staying close.
Sometimes it means encouraging someone to seek appropriate help.
Sometimes it means setting wise boundaries.
Sometimes it means admitting that you, too, need someone to hold up your hands.
And that last admission can be the hardest.
Especially for people who have built their entire identity around being strong.
You know how to encourage others.
You know what Scriptures to quote.
You know how to pray for the hurting.
You know how to tell people that God is faithful.
But when someone asks how you are doing, you automatically answer:
“I'm okay.”
Even when you are not.
Even when the battle has lasted longer than you expected.
Even when the smile on your face has become a carefully practiced disguise.
Maybe you have been so determined to look spiritually mature that you have forgotten how to be spiritually honest.
Moses did not become less significant because he needed Aaron and Hur.
And you do not become less loved by God because you need help.
There is no shame in acknowledging the limits of your humanity.
But there is danger in pretending you have no limits at all.
And now, we must look beyond the hill.
Because although Hur's faithfulness is worth remembering, Hur is not the ultimate hero of the Bible.
Neither is Moses.
Neither is Joshua.
The Scriptures ultimately lead us to Jesus Christ.
And we need to approach that connection carefully.
Exodus 17 does not explicitly identify Hur as a prophetic symbol of Jesus, nor does it teach that the raised hands of Moses directly predict the crucifixion.
We should not force details into the passage that the biblical author does not state.
Yet within the larger story of redemption, Exodus 17 reminds us of a truth that becomes gloriously clear in the New Testament.
God's people are dependent upon divine deliverance.
Human leaders grow weary.
Human strength fails.
Human helpers, however faithful, remain limited.
But Jesus Christ is the perfect Savior.
Hebrews 7:25 declares:
“Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.”
Consider that.
Moses' hands became heavy.
But Jesus Christ, our risen High Priest, lives forever to intercede for His people.
Aaron and Hur helped sustain Moses for a battle that lasted until sunset.
But the saving work of Jesus reaches beyond a single battlefield, beyond a single generation, and into eternity.
At Calvary, Christ bore the judgment our sins deserved.
He was not merely another exhausted leader who needed assistance.
He was the sinless Son of God who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
He suffered.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The victory over sin and death is not something we achieve by holding our hands high enough or by surrounding ourselves with sufficiently strong friends.
It is grounded in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
That is why our deepest hope cannot rest in finding a perfect Hur.
People can love us deeply and still disappoint us.
Friends may move away.
Leaders may fail.
Family members may misunderstand us.
The people who once supported us may themselves become exhausted.
But Christ remains faithful.
His grace does not depend upon our ability to impress Him.
His forgiveness is not purchased by our religious performance.
His salvation is not a reward for people who have successfully hidden every weakness.
It is God's gift to sinners who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast.
And that brings us to the scandal.
Not a scandal Scripture attributes to Hur.
The scandal of our own condition before a holy God.
The selfishness we excuse.
The pride we protect.
The bitterness we nurse.
The secret sins we keep hidden behind respectable Christian appearances.
The moments when we would rather receive glory than give it to God.
The times we have watched another believer struggle and chosen criticism instead of compassion.
Perhaps you have been wounded by people who should have supported you.
Perhaps you have wounded others when they needed you most.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to prove that you are strong enough, holy enough, useful enough, or important enough to deserve God's love.
But the Gospel announces something radically different.
You cannot earn the grace that Jesus freely offers.
You cannot undo your sins through enough religious activity.
You need a Savior. And His name is Jesus.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had learned to look strong.
Not after we had become useful to a ministry.
Not after we had finally convinced everyone that we were doing fine.
Christ died for sinners.
And when a sinner comes to Him in genuine repentance and faith, grace begins a transformation no human applause could ever produce.
The proud learn humility.
The bitter learn forgiveness.
The selfish learn generosity.
The isolated discover the beauty of Christian fellowship.
The wounded learn that their pain does not have to become their identity.
The fallen discover that their past does not have to dictate their future.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It does not mean healing always happens quickly.
It does not mean the Christian life becomes free from hardship.
It means that through Jesus Christ, forgiveness and new life are truly possible.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the story of Hur becomes even more meaningful when we return to the battlefield one final time.
Picture the long hours.
The relentless struggle below.
The heat of the day.
The stone beneath Moses.
Aaron on one side.
Hur on the other.
We do not know exactly what words they exchanged.
We do not know whether Hur's own arms began to ache.
We do not know whether the hours felt endless.
The Bible leaves those details unspoken.
But we know that they continued supporting Moses until sunset.
And that is the part we must not rush past.
They did not merely begin helping. They remained faithful through the battle.
It is relatively easy to offer encouragement when somebody first announces a crisis.
It is harder to keep showing up when the crisis lasts for months.
It is easy to say, “I'm praying for you,” when a story first breaks your heart.
It is harder to remember that person when the excitement has faded and everyone else has moved on.
It is easy to celebrate someone else's calling when their success does not inconvenience you.
It is harder to serve when their assignment requires your sacrifice.
But love that reflects Christ is more than a moment of emotion.
It becomes visible in faithful action.
The Apostle Paul writes in Philippians 2:3–4 that believers should reject selfish ambition and look not only to their own interests but also to the interests of others.
Then he points them to the humility of Jesus Christ.
That is the foundation of Christian service.
Not guilt.
Not public pressure.
Not the promise of recognition.
Not the fear that God will reject us if we fail to do enough.
Love shaped by the Gospel.
Because Christ first loved us.
Maybe today you are Moses.
You are weary.
You have responsibilities that feel heavier than you expected.
You need someone trustworthy to come alongside you.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not have to pretend that your hands are steady when they are shaking.
Reach out to a mature believer.
Speak honestly with someone you trust.
Ask for prayer.
Receive practical help when it is offered.
Your weakness does not disqualify you from receiving God's care.
Maybe today you are Aaron.
You have been standing beside someone for a long time.
You have seen their struggles up close.
You know how much the responsibility costs them.
Do not underestimate the gift of your steady presence.
And maybe today you are Hur.
You are not the person everyone notices.
You are not the one receiving public congratulations.
You are simply doing what love requires.
You keep showing up.
You keep encouraging.
You keep serving.
You keep praying.
And sometimes you wonder whether any of it matters.
It matters.
Not because you are secretly the hero of somebody else's salvation.
Only Jesus saves.
But because God calls His people to love one another, and He can use ordinary faithfulness in extraordinary ways.
One day, the work you performed in obscurity may bear fruit you never expected.
Or you may never see its full impact in this lifetime.
Either way, your obedience is not meaningless.
And perhaps the most searching question of this entire story is not whether you have someone to hold up your hands.
Perhaps it is this:
Whose trembling hands have you noticed but not yet reached out to support?
The elderly believer who has stopped attending church because nobody offers to help them get there.
The single parent who is quietly overwhelmed.
The young Christian struggling with temptation and afraid to confess it.
The missionary who rarely hears from the people who promised to pray.
The friend whose faith is being tested by grief.
The family member you have been meaning to call.
You may not be able to solve their entire situation.
You may not have the money, wisdom, time, or strength to change everything.
But perhaps you can offer something real.
A prayer.
A meal.
A conversation.
An act of service.
A word of Scripture spoken with tenderness and truth.
A reminder that they have not been abandoned.
And when you do, remember whose name must be lifted highest.
Not yours.
Not theirs.
The LORD is our banner.
That is also the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not to build a personality around a platform, but to keep pointing people to the Savior who alone can forgive sins, restore broken lives, and transform hearts.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who are carrying battles they have never told anyone about.
Some have drifted from the faith.
Some have been wounded by churches or other Christians.
Some have grown comfortable with sin.
Some are seeking God but do not know where to begin.
Some are believers who desperately need biblical encouragement.
And some may encounter the message of Jesus through an article that a friend cared enough to share.
That is why your participation matters.
Add a few sincere words about why it matters to you.
Not to promote a human name.
Not to prove your spirituality.
But because someone in your circle may need to hear that Jesus Christ is still the answer for weary, sinful, broken people.
And if someone comes to mind who is struggling privately, consider sending the article to them personally, with compassion rather than pressure.
There may come a day when you need to remember that even Moses needed help—and that the Lord remains faithful when His servants become tired.
And I want to invite you into something more personal.
Are you the exhausted Moses who needs someone to pray for you?
Are you the quiet Hur who has been supporting others while fighting your own unseen battles?
Or has God brought someone to mind whom you need to help?
And if this message has exposed pride, neglect, bitterness, or a need to return to the Lord, you can write:
You do not need to disclose private struggles publicly to prove your sincerity. God hears the prayer you cannot put into words, too.
But if you choose to share, your honest testimony may encourage another person who thought they were struggling alone.
Our desire is to keep bringing Scripture-centered teaching, Gospel encouragement, conviction, repentance, discipleship, and reminders of the grace found in Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for truth.
But there is another way you can stand alongside this work.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity must come from a willing heart.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
We want that principle to remain central.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not the suggestion that you must pay to glorify God.
You can glorify God through faithful obedience, prayer, loving service, sharing the Gospel, and generosity according to your ability.
These items are simply an added benefit. The greater purpose is to support a continuing mission of biblical encouragement and discipleship.
You can still pray for the ministry.
You can still encourage someone who is struggling.
And you can still make a genuine difference in another person's life.
Because Christian service is not measured only by financial giving.
Sometimes the gift is a donation.
Sometimes the gift is a shared message.
Sometimes the gift is an hour of your time.
Sometimes the gift is an arm extended toward someone who can no longer hold their own hands up.
And sometimes the most important gift you can offer another person is to point them away from yourself and toward Jesus.
That is where everything must lead.
Back to Christ.
Back to His Word.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
Back to the cross.
Back to the empty tomb.
Back to the Savior who is worthy of every ounce of glory.
So before you leave this story, remember that battlefield.
Remember the weary hands.
Remember the stone.
Remember Aaron.
Remember Hur.
Remember Joshua fighting below.
And above all, remember the altar Moses built when the victory was won.
The LORD is my banner.
Not my strength.
Not my reputation.
Not my ministry.
Not my sacrifice.
Not the number of people who notice what I have done.
The Lord.
It is to turn from sin and trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
Come to Him honestly.
Bring your guilt.
Bring your pride.
Bring your failures.
Bring the secret you have been hiding.
Bring the exhaustion you can no longer disguise.
You will not find salvation in your ability to hold everything together.
You will find salvation in Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
And if you already belong to Him, ask the Lord to make you more like Christ.
More humble.
More faithful.
More willing to serve.
More willing to receive help.
More eager to see His name glorified than your own.
Because the world may remember the person holding the staff.
But the Lord sees the people faithfully serving beside them.
And when the battle finally ends, the greatest reward will never be hearing the crowd applaud our names.
It will be knowing that we belonged to Jesus and served Him faithfully.
You may be forgotten by the crowd on the battlefield, but you are never unseen by the Savior who carried the cross for you.
